text: Unit 1, 1.1. Today on The World Close-Up, the 51,500 kilometer fruit salad. Thanks to globalization, many things are now available to us that simply weren't available before. On last week's program, we talked about how people around the world are watching TV programs from overseas, wearing clothes from other countries, and working at companies with several international offices. On this week's program, let's look at how globalization allows us to taste food from different cultures around the world, without leaving our own country. We don't just mean specialty products, like Turkish sweets and Japanese snacks. Think about the regular food products customers buy every day. Where do they come from? How do they get to your supermarket? And what is the true environmental cost of your usual shopping list? Our reporter Darren Hayes has gone to a fresh mart in central London to investigate this issue, and to see just what countries customers are putting in their baskets. Hello, I'm here at the fresh mart in central London. There are a lot of healthy consumers here, and David Green is one of them. David, can we take a look in your basket? What are you buying today? Mostly fruit and vegetables. I've got a bunch of grapes, some bananas, some kiwis, a small packet of blueberries. I'm making a fruit salad for lunch as I'm trying to eat healthily. I'm also buying some tomatoes and a lettuce. I notice on the label that the bananas are from Colombia. Yeah? So? Do you mind if I check the grapes? Okay, so these are from South Africa. The kiwis come from New Zealand, and the blueberries are from Argentina. So, in fact, all of this fruit is imported from overseas. Well, I guess as it's winter we can't grow these fruits in our country. They have to be imported. If they weren't, then how would we get fresh fruit in winter? Good point. The global food industry, importing fresh foods by air, ship, rail or road, allows people all over the world to eat a huge variety of fresh fruit and vegetables all year round. It's just more convenient, isn't it? Most of the fruit and vegetables I like, like peppers, oranges and bananas, grow in hotter climates. A lot of the fruit and veg that grow here in the UK is so boring. It is possible to grow some fruit and vegetables from warmer countries here throughout the year, but they have to grow in greenhouses, which increases production costs. If you look at these tomatoes, which were grown on a local farm, they're almost twice the cost of the tomatoes you have here from Morocco, over 3,500 km away. I'd never pay that for a few tomatoes. Local food can be so expensive. It's not worth it. Well, maybe, but let's look at some other figures. The bananas from Colombia must have traveled more than 8,500 km to reach Fresh Mart. The grapes from South Africa must have come more than 9,600 km. And the Argentinian blueberries nearly 11,100 km. The kiwis from New Zealand? They must have flown about 18,800 km. So that's about 51,500 km of air travel in one bowl. Some people would say that's an incredibly long food supply chain. They would also say it has a huge carbon footprint, which means a huge amount of pollution was produced to get this food to the shelves. When food travels, a lot of carbon dioxide is produced. And it's generally accepted that carbon dioxide in the air is causing climate change, causing the earth to get generally warmer. I've never really thought about it that much. What about this lettuce? It's local? Yes, it's grown locally. However, most supermarkets have several large factories all over the country. So after food is picked, it's often transported to large factories to be packaged and sold. This lettuce may be local, but the farm it came from could have transported it across the country and then put it into this plastic packaging. It's sometimes then transported back to the place it was grown in the first place. So before arriving at Fresh Mart, this local lettuce might have traveled... Maybe up to 500 km? You can only really be sure how far something has traveled if you purchase it directly from a farm or if you grow it yourself. Wow! I can't believe it. Maybe I should take up gardening and grow my own food. Oh, but then I wouldn't have nearly as much variety in what I eat. We can have a 51,500 km fruit salad that comes from four different countries and it might not seem very expensive to the consumer. But the big question is, what's the true environmental cost of such well-traveled food? Thanks for your time, David. That's all for today. Thanks for listening to The World Close Up.
